questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Conjunct and disjunct motion
questions.learningObjective: classify a melodic motion as conjunct or disjunct from the size of its intervals
questions.explanation: Conjunct motion means the line moves by step, that is by seconds, and disjunct motion means it leaps, that is by a third or anything larger. The C4, D4, E4, F4 opening is a chain of seconds and is therefore conjunct, while F4 up to B4 spans six semitones, which is a tritone, and is unmistakably a leap. The convention is a property of the individual interval rather than of the whole line, so a melody can mix the two freely and is usually described by whichever dominates. The reading that treats every interval as fillable is describing potential rather than what is written, and a line that turns direction is not thereby disqualified from being conjunct.
questions.hint: Look at the size of each individual interval rather than at the shape of the line.

options.text: The first four notes are conjunct and the leap is disjunct, since it spans more than a second
Both are conjunct, since every interval in a melody can be filled with intermediate notes
options.misconception: equates what could be written with what is written, ignoring the size of the leap

options.text: Both are disjunct, since a line that changes direction cannot be called conjunct at all
options.misconception: thinks a change of direction disqualifies stepwise motion, which it does not

options.text: The first is disjunct and the leap conjunct, since conjunct motion covers intervals of any size
options.misconception: reverses the two terms, so the labels are attached to the wrong motions

questions.topic: Filling a leap with scale steps
questions.learningObjective: count the notes needed to fill a melodic leap with steps of the scale
questions.explanation: A filled fifth in C major runs C4, D4, E4, F4, G4, which is five notes, and the two end notes are not inserted notes, so 5 minus 2 is 3, namely D4, E4 and F4. The second route counts steps instead of notes: the leap spans four letter names, C, D, E, F, G, so a filled line makes four steps, and four steps need three notes between the endpoints. Both routes agree. The number 3 is also what makes the figure sound like one gesture rather than a leap followed by three separate notes. The trap is 5, which is the count of notes in the filled line including its two endpoints.
questions.hint: Count the note names in the filled line, then subtract the two end notes.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting changes of direction in a contour
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that counts the direction changes of a melodic line
questions.explanation: The line has five intervals whose directions are plus, minus, plus, minus, plus, and a change can only occur where two intervals meet, so there are four such meetings and every one of them is a change, giving 4. The shape is therefore a zig-zag: the line rises, falls, rises, falls and rises again without ever settling. The figure 5 is the trap, because five is the number of intervals rather than the number of changes, and a change needs two intervals to define it. The last reading inverts the meaning of contour, which is precisely the record of these reversals, so a line with many of them has a strong contour rather than none.
questions.hint: Work out the direction of each interval first, then count the meetings where the sign changes.

options.misconception: counts one reversal fewer than the line actually makes, stopping before the last meeting

options.text: 5, describing a line whose direction changes once for each of its five intervals
options.misconception: counts intervals rather than the meetings between them, which is the off-by-one trap

options.text: 0, describing a line that reverses so often that it has no overall contour to report

questions.topic: Reading a contour report and locating the climax
questions.learningObjective: interpret a contour report and say where the line's climax falls
questions.explanation: The intervals of the line rise, fall, rise, rise, rise, fall and rise, so the shape is upward overall with reversals at the second, sixth and seventh intervals, giving four changes of direction, and the final note C5 is the highest pitch in the line. A climax in the final position means the line has no descending tail: the tension built by the reversals is never released before the music stops, which is why such a melody sounds like it is arriving rather than concluding. The claim of conjunct motion ignores the drop from D4 to B3, which is a fourth, and four reversals in eight notes leaves ample room for leaps rather than removing them.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What a rising and a falling line convey
questions.learningObjective: state the conventional affect of rising and falling melodic motion
questions.explanation: The meanings are conventions learned from tonal practice rather than physical facts, and they come from where lines tend to go. Rising lines have momentum, and the commonest rise of all is the stepwise approach to the tonic or to its octave, so a rising line tends to sound like approach or arrival. Falling lines lose momentum and commonly settle on a note of stability, so they tend to sound like conclusion. None of this is compulsory: a rising line can be anxious and a falling one can be decisive, which is why a composer who wants an unusual effect can reverse the expectation deliberately. What is wrong is the claim that the two are identical, since the conventions exist even though they can be overridden.
questions.hint: Think about where such lines usually end up in tonal music rather than about the shape alone.

options.text: A rising line suggests growth or arrival, and a falling line suggests settling or decline
A rising line suggests tension or anxiety, and a falling line suggests calm and release
options.misconception: reverses the conventions, giving falling lines the energy they normally lack

options.text: The two shapes carry the same sense, since contour is a matter of taste rather than convention
options.misconception: denies that conventions exist, though listeners rely on them constantly

options.text: A rising line is neutral, and only a falling line is able to carry any affect at all
options.misconception: assigns all expression to falling lines and rules out rising ones entirely

A third route counts the changes directly, one meeting at a time, and finds the same four. The trap is 5, which is the number of intervals rather than the number of changes, since a change of direction is defined by two intervals meeting.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Measuring the size of a melodic leap
questions.learningObjective: count the semitones spanned by a named melodic leap
questions.explanation: The chromatic table from C4 runs C, C sharp, D, D sharp, E, F, F sharp, G, G sharp, A, which is ten names and nine steps, so the answer is 9. The second route is the octave: an octave holds 12 semitones and the same pair of notes read downward, from A4 to the C above it, is a minor third of 3, so 9 and 3 must make 12 and the leap is 9. The letter count agrees, since C, D, E, F, G and A is six names and a sixth in C major is a major sixth of 9 semitones. Since 9 is well over a third, the motion is disjunct, which is the practical point of the measurement.
questions.hint: Walk the chromatic table up from the lower note and confirm with the octave complement.

questions.topic: Filling an octave with scale steps
questions.learningObjective: count the notes needed to fill an octave with successive scale steps
questions.explanation: Filling the octave with scale steps gives C4, D4, E4, F4, G4, A4, B4, C5, which is eight notes, and removing the two end notes leaves 6. The second route counts steps: an octave spans seven letter names from C to the next C, so a filled line makes seven steps and therefore eight notes, and 8 minus 2 is 6. The distinction matters because filling by scale step and filling by semitone are not the same act: a chromatic fill of the same octave would need eleven interior notes, and it is the scale-step fill that a reader means when a leap is described as filled.
questions.hint: Write out the scale notes from the lower note up to the octave and count the interior ones.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Telling a contrapuntal texture from a chordal one
questions.learningObjective: interpret a texture report and decide whether the writing is contrapuntal
questions.explanation: Contrapuntal texture is defined by the independence of the voices, and the report gives two direct pieces of evidence: the voices move at different rates, and no two of them change pitch on the same beat, so none of them is a decoration of another. The bass moving only by step or third adds a third, since an independent line avoids the wide leaps that a chordal accompaniment makes when it follows a melody. Homophony would show the opposite pattern, with most voices moving together under a single melody. The reading that calls this monophonic misreads independence as absence, since several distinct lines are plainly sounding at once, and heterophony would require the same melody in several versions rather than different notes in each voice.
questions.hint: Ask whether the voices move at the same times and whether any of them is supporting another.

options.text: Contrapuntal, since the voices move at different rates and none of them decorates another
Homophonic, since the fastest voice is on top and carries the melody the others support
options.misconception: assumes the top voice is a melody supported by others, the opposite of independence

options.text: Monophonic, since no two voices ever move together and so only one line is audible at all
options.misconception: mistakes independence for absence, when four distinct lines are sounding

options.text: Heterophonic, since several versions of one melody would have to be sounding side by side
options.misconception: names a texture that would need the same melody in several versions at once

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Metrical displacement
questions.learningObjective: describe metrical displacement and the accent it puts off the beat
questions.explanation: Metrical displacement happens when a rhythmic unit that belongs on a strong beat is moved to a weak one and keeps its own accent, so the accent no longer coincides with the accent of the metre. The bar still sounds in 4/4, but the listener is made to feel the strong beat somewhere the metre does not put it, and the two patterns rub against each other until the displacement is resolved. Syncopation is the related and more common device of putting an accent on a weak beat, so the second reading is a near neighbour rather than a total stranger; the difference is that displacement relocates a whole unit and its accent together. Hemiola is a different matter, since it regroups three pulses against the bar's own grouping, and tying is a notation device rather than an accentual one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the accent and the unit have both moved away from the beat the metre expects.

options.text: Metrical displacement, and it throws the expected accent onto an offbeat so the metre feels tilted

options.misconception: calls the device by the name of its close neighbour, which shifts only the accent

options.text: Hemiola, and it regroups the bar into three pulses that replace the four of the metre
options.misconception: describes a regrouping of the bar rather than a displacement of one unit

options.text: Tying, and it holds a note across the beat so the accent falls on the note instead of the beat
options.misconception: names a notation device, which produces no accent of its own

questions.topic: Transposing a motive up a given number of semitones
questions.learningObjective: trace a transposition rule and identify the interval a sequence uses
questions.explanation: The pitch classes of the motive are 0, 2, 4 and 5, and adding 3 gives 3, 5, 7 and 8, which are E flat, F, G and A flat, so the sequence sounds E flat 4, F4, G4, A flat 4. The interval of transposition is the 3 that was added, a minor third, and because the same figure is added to every note the intervals between the notes of the motive are unchanged, which is what makes the restatement a transposition and not a new tune. The reading that adds only 1 has picked a chromatic semitone, and the one that adds 2 has produced a whole step whose spelling would make the motive diatonic. The last reading mistakes transposition for a return to the starting pitches.
questions.hint: Add the figure to each pitch class, wrap round the twelve-note table, and keep the intervals.

questions.topic: The interval that transposes a sequence

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: A ground bass and its harmonic work
questions.learningObjective: define a ground bass and state the harmonic function it performs
questions.explanation: A ground bass is a repeating bass pattern, usually a line or a short harmonic sequence, that returns unchanged while everything above it is varied. Its function is harmonic stability: the ground keeps reasserting the harmony and therefore the key, so the listener has a fixed point against which the variations can be heard as departures rather than as new pieces. That is what distinguishes a ground from a pedal, which is a single sustained or reiterated note rather than a pattern, and from a descending-fifths sequence, which is a method of moving away from the key rather than a way of holding it. The doubling reading confuses a bass line with a melodic shadow of the tune.
questions.hint: Ask what stays the same between statements and what changes, and whether the bass is one note or several.

options.text: A doubling of the melody an octave below, which simply reinforces the tune from underneath
options.misconception: confuses a bass line with a shadow of the melody sounding below it

options.text: A pedal, since any bass pattern that returns amounts to a single note being held down

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The exposition of a fugue and its order of entries
questions.learningObjective: name a fugue's exposition and state what fixes the order of its entries
questions.explanation: The exposition is the opening span in which every voice states the subject, the first voice alone and each later voice with an answer or a real restatement, usually accompanied by a countersubject from the second entry onwards. What fixes the order is simply the order in which the composer chooses to bring the voices in, which in the common case runs from the highest voice down to the lowest so that the entries accumulate downwards. The development is the later section that works on the material once the entries are established, and it is not an opening series at all. The alternating pattern named in the last reading confuses a subject with a countersubject, which is a second line sounding at the same time rather than a later entry.
questions.hint: Name the span in which each voice in turn states the subject, and ask what decides who goes first.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What constrains a countersubject
questions.learningObjective: explain why a countersubject must work in more than one key and more than one position
questions.explanation: A countersubject is a melody written to sound against the subject, and the reason it is shaped so carefully is that it will be used again and again in different keys. Its intervals are chosen as a fixed pattern relative to the subject, often a second or a third away in the upper part, because a pattern that repeats will clash in the same way every time and can therefore be moved between keys safely. Position is the second constraint: the line is composed for the voice that first carries it, and its interval content may not suit the bass. The price of this planning is that a countersubject cannot be invented freely whenever a new form of the subject turns up, which is why fugue subjects are freer than their companions.
questions.hint: Ask how many different keys the subject will be stated in, and what a line must do to survive all of them.

answer.exemplar: The second line is the countersubject, and the constraint on it is that it must combine well with the subject in more than one place. A subject is stated in several keys during a fugue, beginning in the tonic and moving to the dominant and beyond, so a countersubject written to fit one key will clash in the next. The usual solution is to write it so that it sits at a fixed interval above the subject, because a consistent relationship of intervals produces a consistent dissonance pattern and therefore travels between keys intact. A second constraint is position: the countersubject is designed for the voice it first appears in, and moving it to another part may leave gaps or crossings, so a composer who wants it everywhere writes a countersubject that is invertible. What the composer gives up is independence of invention, because the countersubject can no longer be composed freely against a later, different form of the subject. The wrong belief to avoid is that the countersubject is a second theme of equal importance: it exists to be combined with the subject, and it is usually the least memorable part of a fugue for that reason.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: How a fugue reaches its final cadence
questions.learningObjective: explain how a fugue's closing cadence is built from its own entries
questions.explanation: A fugue's ending is prepared by compression rather than by contrast. A stretto in the closing passage sets the entries closer and closer together, which creates an accumulating urgency; the composer then stops adding voices, and the ear hears the texture thin until only the cadence is left. Into that space the subject is usually quoted in the tonic, so the material the work has been about is also the material that confirms the key. The remaining requirement is a proper cadence with the leading tone resolving and the tonic in the outer voices, since a fugue that simply stops leaves the dominant's obligation unpaid. A coda can follow, but the cadence is part of the counterpoint, not an appendage to it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the spacing of the entries just before the ending, and which line returns in the tonic.

answer.exemplar: The cadence of a fugue is normally built out of the counterpoint that already exists, so the ending is a consequence of the form rather than an addition to it. Two devices do most of the work. The first is the stretto: by running the entries close together, usually in a final passage where the last entry of the subject overlaps the one before it, the composer builds momentum and then withdraws the entries one by one, so that the texture thins out audibly. The second is the reprise of the subject, often its first few notes, in the tonic, which puts the principal material of the work into the key that is finally being confirmed. What the entries must then contribute is the leading tone, so that the dominant sonority still has its obligation unresolved at the moment of the cadence, and a soprano line that arrives on the tonic rather than on the third or the fifth. The wrong belief to avoid is that a fugue needs a separate closing section; a coda may follow, but the cadence itself belongs to the entries, and a fugue that stops without one sounds as though it has been interrupted.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The performance convention of a minuet and trio
questions.learningObjective: explain the performance convention governing a minuet and trio movement
questions.explanation: Two conventions attach to the movement. The first is the repeat scheme, in which the minuet is played twice, the second time only as far as the trio, and the trio is then played twice, giving the order one, one, two, two. The second is historical: the name trio comes from having three instruments or three players take the middle section while the rest of the company danced the minuet, which is why the section was written lighter in texture than the dance it follows. Musically the two sections share their rhythmic material, so the trio's faster triple metre is a change of pace within one dance rather than a change of subject, and that is why the return of the minuet afterwards carries weight. What the trio is not is a separate movement or a fugue in disguise.
questions.hint: Separate the repeat scheme from the name's origin, then consider what the two sections share musically.

answer.exemplar: The convention concerns both repeats and dancers. Structurally, the minuet and trio divides into two parts, a minuet in a slow triple metre and a trio in a faster triple metre, and the traditional scheme is to play the minuet twice, the second time only as far as the trio, and then to play the trio twice as well, so that the movement is heard in the order one, one, two, two. The word trio comes from the practice of having three instruments, or three players, play that section during the dance while the whole company danced the minuet, so the name records an older convention rather than the number of voices present today. Musically the two sections are built from the same rhythmic material, so the faster trio is not a new piece but the same dance with its pulse lifted, and the return of the minuet afterwards therefore sounds like a homecoming rather than a change of subject. The wrong belief to avoid is that the trio is a separate movement, or that it is always lighter in texture, which is common but not defining: what defines it is the faster triple metre and the repeat scheme.

questions.topic: Phrase rhythm and its grouping
questions.learningObjective: explain how long and short notes group a melody into phrases
questions.explanation: Phrase rhythm is the way note values are distributed so that the melody falls into groups a listener can hear as units, and it works with the accents to make those groups audible. Eight notes with accents on 1, 3, 5 and 7 present four equal pairs, so the phrase is heard as four short gestures; the same notes with the accents concentrated on 1 and 5 are heard as two longer phrases. The underlying metre matters too, and a note value that crosses the barline or displaces a strong beat makes the listener feel the grouping against the pulse, which is the source of syncopation. The mistaken belief is that a phrase has a fixed length, since the same notes regroup simply by moving where the long values and accents fall.
questions.hint: Look at where the long notes and the accents sit, and try the same notes with the accents in different places.

answer.exemplar: Phrase rhythm is the pattern of long and short notes in a melody, and it works together with the underlying metre to tell a listener how the notes group into phrases. Where the rhythm cooperates with the metre the grouping is heard without effort, and where it crosses the metre the listener hears a displacement. The grouping is not fixed by the number of notes: the same eight notes can be heard as four pairs or as two groups of four, and which grouping is heard depends on where the long notes and the accents fall. With accents on notes 1, 3, 5 and 7 and longer values there, the ear is offered four equally weighted groups of two, so the melody sounds like four short gestures that begin and end with the same question-and-answer shape. Redistribute the accents so that notes 1 and 5 carry them strongly and notes 3 and 7 weakly, keeping the same notes, and the same eight notes sound like two larger phrases. The wrong belief to avoid is that a phrase is a fixed number of bars, since phrasing is a matter of grouping and a phrase of four bars and a phrase of eight bars can be made from identical material by changing where the long notes fall.

questions.explanation: A theme followed by restatements of itself in which something other than the outline changes is a set of theme and variations, and the count of statements is one more than the count of variations, so nine statements of 32 bars. The rondo is the nearest error, because a rondo also has a recurring section, but its episodes are contrasting material rather than varied versions of the refrain, and they are usually of different lengths. The development reading is wrong because a development belongs inside a larger form and is not a series of equal statements, and the fugue reading confuses a theme that survives alteration with one that is imitated by a new voice entering later.
questions.hint: Ask whether each statement after the first is new material or a changed version of the same melody.

options.text: A theme and variations, since one melody is restated again and again with a different feature changed
A rondo, since a returning theme between contrasting sections always makes a set of variations
A development, since the sections after the first are the working-out of the opening idea
A fugue, since keeping an outline audible while changing its surface is the definition of imitation

questions.topic: A claim about a key that the cadence contradicts
questions.learningObjective: judge a key claim against the closing chords an analysis reports
questions.explanation: A cadence names a key through its pair of chords, not through its last chord alone. A minor to E major is the first chord on the tonic followed by the chord on the dominant of A minor, so the pair belongs to A minor, and the claim that the final chord is the tonic of A major is impossible because E is the fifth degree of A, not its first. In A major the tonic would be A major itself, and the dominant is also E major, so the second chord alone is ambiguous between the two keys and only the first chord settles the matter. Ending on a dominant is possible and is what a half cadence does, but it would not normally be the last chord of a movement, and in any case it would make the writer's claim worse rather than better.
questions.hint: Read the two chords together as a cadence and ask which of them is the tonic of which key.

options.text: The claim is contradicted, since a cadence from A minor to E major settles in A minor, not A major
The claim is supported, since a piece may end on its dominant when the writer wants an open ending
options.misconception: grants the claim on the strength of the last chord alone, ignoring the first

options.text: The analysis is wrong, since a minor chord may never move to the major chord a fourth above it
options.misconception: forbids the commonest cadence in music, which is minor to its own dominant

options.text: Nothing follows, since a closing cadence in one key says nothing whatever about the key of a work
options.misconception: denies that a cadence identifies a key, which is what cadences are for
